extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy (readers of Aristotle / ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and conceptual analysis of Justice (Book V of Aristotle's Ethics), enumerating and distinguishing species of justice, conditions of just/unjust actions, and related juridical/economic principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive Justice (proportionate distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: That which concerns the distribution of common property according to proportion: if the division is made out of common property, the shares will bear the same proportion to one another as the original contributions did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematicians call this geometrical proportion (the whole to the whole as each part to each part). Example and formulation: A : B :: C : D; when distributing, terms must be combined so as to preserve the same ratio. Violating this proportion constitutes the Unjust in distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective Justice (restorative/arithmetic equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The species of Just that arises in transactions between men and is an equal in an arithmetical sense; it aims to restore equality where one party has gained and another lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Just is the mean between loss and gain; judges restore equality by taking from the greater that which it exceeds the mean and adding it to the less. Examples: robbery, assault — the judge endeavours to reduce unequal shares to equality via penalty or compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a Mean (general characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is a mean state that aims at producing the mean between excess and defect with respect to the proportionate; it differs from other virtues because it produces the mean rather than being a mean state 'in the same manner'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting justly is the mean between acting unjustly (having more) and being acted upon unjustly (having less).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocation must be proportional (not exact equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocation binds exchange relations but must be according to proportion rather than strict equality; proportionate reciprocity holds the social community together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In exchange (e.g., builder and shoemaker) goods must be equalised by proportion before exchange. Exact one-for-one reciprocity (tit-for-tat) fails for distributive and corrective justice; reciprocity of good preserves participation, reciprocity of evil is servile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money / Commensurability as prerequisite for exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: All things that can be exchanged should be capable of comparison; money is a conventional medium that measures all things and makes exchange possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money is a representative of Demand by general agreement (vo/loko-jua); it equalises heterogeneous goods by assigning prices so that exchange can occur at any time. Example: determining how many shoes equal a house using money as a measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Voluntary vs Involuntary acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary actions are those done with knowledge and in the agent's power (absence of ignorance about person, instrument, result) and not by compulsion; involuntary are done through ignorance or compulsion or not in the agent's control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: if another seizes your hand and strikes, the owner of the hand did not act voluntarily. Voluntariness affects whether an act is judged just/unjust in character or only accidentally so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: mistake vs misadventure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a hurt occurs contrary to all reasonable expectation it is a misadventure; when it occurs without viciousness but from an origin that rests with the agent it is a mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistake: agent originates the cause (e.g., wrong instrument/target/result without viciousness). Misadventure: cause external to agent. This distinction informs excusability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate choice vs passion/impulse (formation of character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts done from deliberate choice (deliberation) that embody the Unjust make the agent a confirmed unjust character; acts from passion or without prior deliberation can be unjust actions but need not form an unjust character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adultery or theft done in sudden passion is unjust act but may not make one an adulterer/thief in character. Anger-driven acts are judged not to be malice prepense because the originator is the provocateur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excusable vs inexcusable involuntary harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Involuntary harms are either excusable (errors from ignorance) or not excusable (those done in ignorance caused by a passion that is neither natural nor fairly attributable to human infirmity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors due to ignorance may be excused; harms caused by non-natural, blameworthy passion are inexcusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Justice vs Conventional (legal) Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Justs are natural (have the same force everywhere and do not depend on being received) and others are conventional (depend on enactment, custom, or special decree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of conventional: price of ransom fixed by law, specific sacrificial practices. Though both may change, some principles have a natural basis even among humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between abstract Just/Unjust and particular acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Just and Unjust as universals bear to the many particular acts the relation of universal to particular; an unjust thing may exist by nature or ordinance, but an unjust act exists only when embodied in voluntary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawful justice and primary/natural justice may not coincide. Terminology note: distinction between generic 'just act' and corrective 'justice' as terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for being 'unjustly dealt with'
rubrics_metrics.description: To be unjustly dealt with requires (in addition to being hurt with knowledge of person/instrument/manner) that the hurt be against the wish of the sufferer; one cannot be unjustly dealt with voluntarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person may suffer something that is unjust in itself voluntarily (e.g., giving property away), but that is not being unjustly dealt with because the suffering is by consent; no man wishes to be hurt, so voluntary being unjustly dealt with is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's office: personification of the Just and method of remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge is the personification of the Just and seeks the mean; his office is to make things equal by taking from the greater that which exceeds the mean and adding it to the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Etymology supports role (Greek terms meaning 'one who divides into two parts'). Judges aim to restore arithmetical equality between parties in corrective justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for determining corrective adjustment (arithmetical illustration)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one of two equal magnitudes has a portion taken and added to the other, the latter exceeds the former by twice the portion; the excess of the mean over the less must be added to the less, and the excess of the greater over the mean be taken from the greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric/arithmetic examples (three equal straight lines, cutting and adding a portion) give a rule to determine how much to take/add to restore equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange requires pre-equalisation of heterogeneous parties
rubrics_metrics.description: No dealing arises between two of the same kind; exchange is between different producers/consumers (physician and agriculturist) who must be equalised in quantity/quality prior to exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If terms are not brought to proportion, extremes will combine exceedings of the mean and the connection (exchange) cannot stand. Money as common measure arises to accomplish this equalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity of goods vs reciprocity of evil and social cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual giving in due proportion (reciprocity of good) is essential to union/participation among citizens; reciprocity of evil is rejected as servile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temple-of-Graces moral: requital of favours creates further benevolence; absence of reciprocation of good prevents admission to participation which is the bond of union.
